synopsis: TacWAM trains one multimodal generator to predict visual futures, tactile futures, and robot action chunks. Its distinctive constraint is that actions read current sensory anchors but cannot read future prediction tokens. Tactile forecasting therefore supplies training supervision rather than an online correction signal or an action-conditioned simulator. The reported physical evaluation reaches 75.0% average task success, versus 37.5% for the strongest evaluated baseline. Staged ablations support the complete design, but do not isolate every proposed mechanism. [e03, e06, e10, e12, e14, e15]

problem.text: The authors argue that visual prediction provides weak supervision for contact mechanics: similar images can conceal different force buildup, deformation, shear, or slip conditions. TacWAM seeks a tactile prediction space that preserves these signals while preventing target-derived future information from becoming an action-learning shortcut.

contributions.text: A single-frame tactile representation combines spatially registered appearance, dense force, and deformation flow, with bilateral force and torque reconstruction supplying global mechanics supervision.
Recent tactile history conditions future tactile prediction through adaptive normalization, while an explicit attention mask separates observable anchors from sensory prediction targets.
The authors demonstrate higher physical task success than four evaluated baseline families and interpret staged degradation as support for tactile history and restricted future-token visibility.

inputs: Current overhead and wrist-camera observations, task/language conditioning, and seven-dimensional joint-position state.
Synchronized bilateral tactile appearance, dense force fields, and mesh deformation flow.
A 32-step window of observed tactile latents, including the current observation, for the tactile prediction expert.
outputs: A 32-step sequence of target joint-position states for robot execution.
Future visual predictions and future 128-dimensional tactile latents.
Optional decoded tactile force, deformation, and bilateral wrench predictions for analysis.

steps.name: Construct the tactile prediction space
steps.detail: SAF encodes each sensor's appearance with a frozen Wan VAE and force/flow with convolutional branches. Features are spatially aligned, fused per side, combined bilaterally, pooled, and mapped to a 128-dimensional latent. A decoder reconstructs dense force, deformation flow, and a 12-dimensional bilateral wrench. Wrench is a reconstruction target, not an additional spatial input; the latent is not claimed to be the full physical state.

steps.name: Summarize recent contact evolution
steps.detail: A temporal residual Conv1d encoder processes 32 tactile latents. Last, mean, maximum, and standard-deviation pooling feed a 256-dimensional context vector. This vector modulates only the tactile expert through its timestep/adaptive-normalization pathway; it is not added as attention-memory tokens.

steps.name: Generate through modality-specific experts
steps.detail: One Mixture-of-Transformers generator contains visual, tactile, and action experts communicating through masked mixed self-attention. Language and current proprioception enter through expert cross-attention. Current visual and tactile observations are anchors; future sensory tokens are noised variables during flow-matching training.

steps.name: Restrict information flow
steps.detail: Actions can read the current visual anchor, current tactile anchor, and all action tokens. They cannot read sensory futures. Visual tokens cannot read tactile tokens. Future tactile tokens read the visual anchor and tactile sequence, but no action tokens. The tactile anchor reads only itself within its stream; future tactile tokens can read the entire tactile sequence, so this is not ordinary token-by-token causal forecasting. Tactile futures are consequently parallel predictions rather than consequences conditioned on proposed actions.

training.text: Stage 1 trains SAF and its decoder with SmoothL1 reconstruction on normalized force, wrench, and flow targets, weighted 1.0, 1.5, and 1.0. The appearance VAE remains frozen. Both SAF and its decoder are frozen after this stage.

Stage 2 trains the generator and history encoder with video, action, and tactile-latent flow-matching losses. A frozen but differentiable decoder supplies semantic consistency gradients to predicted tactile latents. Tactile prediction and decoded consistency exclude the clean anchor. A contact-event auxiliary head predicts six binary labels; stable contact/no-contact uses a duration threshold of eight steps.

Both stages use AdamW, learning rate 1×10−4, cosine scheduling, weight decay 1×10−2, 20 epochs, bfloat16, and seed 42. Per-GPU batch sizes are 32 and 8, with accumulation 1 and 2 respectively. Stage 2 initializes from the Wan2.2-TI2V-5B MoT setup and an aligned ActionDiT checkpoint.
Training data contain 300 demonstrations per task, averaging approximately 500 frames per episode, synchronized at 30 Hz. An explicit demonstration train/validation/test partition is not documented.

inference.text: Default generation uses 20 flow-matching denoising steps. The robot executes a complete 32-step action chunk, acquires new observations, and predicts the next chunk. Each action is a next-transition joint-position target, not an instantaneous force command. Video training geometry contains the current frame and eight future frames after temporal subsampling.

Decoded tactile futures are diagnostic outputs and are not used for online action correction. The demonstrated feedback loop operates between executed chunks; no candidate-action search or tactile rollout-based planner is described.

equations.explanation: Equation (3) summarizes action conditioning on current vision, encoded touch, proprioception, and task information. F_A denotes an information pathway within the shared generator, not a separately specified network. Noised action variables and the flow timestep are omitted in the paper's shorthand.
Equation (10) summarizes recent observed touch into chunk-level context. T_hist is 32; the history endpoint is also the clean tactile anchor for predicting the next chunk.

equations.expression: L_TacWAM = λ_v L_video + λ_a L_action + λ_z L_tac-latent + λ_sem L_tac-decoded + λ_c L_contact.
equations.explanation: Equations (12)/(17) combine three scheduler-weighted flow-matching MSE terms with decoded tactile MSE and contact-event BCE. The respective weights are 1.0, 1.0, 1.0, 0.5, and 0.1. Decoded supervision constrains predicted latents without updating decoder parameters.

results.setting: 20 physical trials per task and method; one final checkpoint; common demonstration data, success definitions, and test-condition sequence.
results.comparison: VT-WAM: 37.5%, the strongest average baseline; reported improvement: 37.5 percentage points.
results.interpretation: Measured robot execution success supports the complete system on these tasks. It is not a video or tactile prediction metric.

results.setting: 20 physical trials; success requires placement without breaking or dropping the chip.
results.comparison: RDP: 50.0%, the strongest task baseline; improvement: 40.0 percentage points.
results.interpretation: Shows a substantial observed advantage under the fragile-object success criterion.

results.setting: 20 physical trials; success requires stable placement without dropping or visible crushing.
results.comparison: π0.5: 60.0%, the strongest task baseline; improvement: 10.0 percentage points.
results.interpretation: The smallest observed task-level advantage; statistical uncertainty was not reported.

results.setting: 20 physical trials; sustained board contact and a predefined cleanliness standard are required.
results.comparison: π0.5: 35.0%, the strongest task baseline; improvement: 40.0 percentage points.
results.interpretation: Supports improved completion of a sustained-contact task, without separately measuring pressure accuracy or contact continuity.

results.setting: 20 physical trials; the required twirling motion must finish without the pens falling.
results.comparison: RDP: 35.0%, the strongest task baseline; improvement: 30.0 percentage points.
results.interpretation: Shows improved execution under dynamic bilateral contact on the tested platform.

results.setting: Chip grasping and wiping; 20 physical trials per task and variant; common Stage 2 data, horizons, and optimization.
results.metric: Chip success / wiping success / two-task mean
results.value: Full: 90.0% / 75.0% / 82.5%; without history: 50.0% / 60.0% / 55.0%; without history + Attn-AT: 30.0% / 45.0% / 37.5%; without history + Attn-VT: 10.0% / 5.0% / 7.5%.
results.comparison: Removing history reduces the mean by 27.5 percentage points. Allowing actions to read tactile futures further reduces success; additional visual–tactile exchange produces the lowest result.
results.interpretation: The nested sequence supports the chosen configuration. History removal also disables contact-event supervision, and relaxed masks are tested only without history, limiting independent causal attribution.

limitations.text: Each method uses one final checkpoint and only 20 trials per task. Confidence intervals, significance tests, and retraining-seed variance are absent. Evaluation within predefined initial-condition ranges does not establish transfer to new objects, sensors, or platforms.

The ablations do not independently isolate history from its auxiliary loss, or mask effects from history interactions. No reported ablation removes future-tactile supervision while preserving current tactile conditioning, or separately tests SAF's input modalities. The authors' shortcut explanation is plausible but not directly measured.

The authors report closer force-magnitude and temporal-trend tracking with history. This evidence is qualitative; no numerical forecasting error is reported, and the supplied extraction does not permit independent inspection of the curves.

Shared data and evaluation conditions do not imply matched compute or identical optimization. Baselines have different configurations, including π0.5's action horizon of 33 versus TacWAM's 32, and RDP and VT-WAM are author reimplementations.

The paper reports 30 Hz stream synchronization and 20 denoising steps, but no measured inference latency or throughput. These specifications do not establish real-time generation or the catalog's efficiency characterization.

reproduction.text: The reviewed artifact is v2, with matching catalog identifier, title, and authors. Reproduction should retain this version because the report assesses its finalized attention rules and appendix settings.

The reported setup requires an Agilex Piper, two Xense G1-WS sensors, calibrated and synchronized camera/tactile/joint streams, and pretrained Wan/ActionDiT components. Stage 2 uses eight NVIDIA A800 80GB GPUs; the documented stack includes PyTorch 2.7.1 and CUDA 12.8. Hardware availability alone would not recover the private training data.

Training/inference code is promised upon publication under a research-use license. Raw data, preprocessing and analysis scripts, trained checkpoints, and baseline reimplementation code are excluded. No code was inspected or experiment reproduced in this reading. Exact force thresholds for contact labels, wrench/flow clipping values, numerical test-condition ranges, and the cleanliness cutoff remain unspecified, although the eight-step stability threshold is given.

A focused follow-up would hold current tactile conditioning and contact-event supervision fixed, remove only tactile-future and decoded-consistency losses, and compare physical success across repeated training seeds. This would test the incremental value of predictive tactile supervision more directly than the reported nested ablations.

reasoning.text: The source explicitly describes one tri-modal MoT generator whose modality experts communicate through masked mixed self-attention. This architecture evidence favors a One Model interpretation over the recorded Dual-system label; the judgment does not rest on joint training alone. Its prediction mechanism is joint future/action generation with restricted attention and auxiliary tactile supervision, which conflicts with the generic Other mechanisms label. It is not inverse dynamics or an action-conditioned tactile consequence model. Multimodal tactile sensing is supported; efficient inference and real-time control remain unverified. Without supplied quadrant definitions, a replacement named quadrant cannot be established. The recorded snapshot is preserved for editorial review.

discussionQuestions: With current tactile conditioning held fixed, how much improvement comes specifically from future-tactile supervision?
Do relaxed masks still degrade performance when tactile history remains enabled, and which parameter pathways transfer tactile prediction supervision into action learning?
What chunk-generation latency is measured on deployment hardware, and how does reducing denoising steps affect physical success?

evidence.location: PDF p. 1, title page and arXiv version stamp
evidence.detail: The title, identifier, and six authors match the catalog. The stamp identifies 2607.28391v2, 24 August 2026; the manuscript date is 6 August 2026.
The authors motivate tactile predictive supervision through mechanically different contacts that can look similar, while requiring action conditioning to remain deployment-available.

evidence.location: PDF pp. 3–4, Sections 3.1–3.2, Eqs. (1)–(3); p. 13, Appendix A.1
evidence.detail: The formulation distinguishes stream conditioning within one tri-modal MoT generator, defines actions as next-state targets, and describes tactile latents as tactile-observable representations rather than full physical states.

evidence.location: PDF p. 4, Section 3.3, Eqs. (4)–(6); pp. 13–14, Appendix A.2; p. 14, Table 4
evidence.detail: SAF aligns appearance, force, and flow features from both sensors into a 128-dimensional latent. Its decoder reconstructs force, flow, and a 12-dimensional wrench. Targets use training-set normalization; wrench/flow clipping is stated without numerical bounds.

evidence.location: PDF p. 5, Section 3.5, Eq. (10); p. 14, Table 4; p. 15, Appendices A.3–A.5
evidence.detail: History uses 32 observed latents and temporal convolutions with four pooling summaries to produce 256-dimensional tactile-expert modulation. Six contact-event labels use BCE with weight 0.1; stability requires eight steps. The force-magnitude threshold is not specified.

evidence.location: PDF p. 5, Section 3.4, Table 1 and Eqs. (7)–(9); pp. 16–17, Appendix B.1–B.4 and Table 5
evidence.detail: AGT permits actions to read only current sensory anchors and action tokens. Future tactile tokens cannot read actions; the clean tactile anchor is protected by the first-frame rule. The paper explicitly characterizes tactile prediction as parallel supervision rather than action-conditioned dynamics.

evidence.location: PDF pp. 5–6, Section 3.6, Eq. (11); p. 17, Appendix C.1, Eq. (16) and Table 6
evidence.detail: Stage 1 uses normalized SmoothL1 force, wrench, and flow reconstruction with weights 1.0, 1.5, and 1.0, then freezes the tactile representation and decoder.

evidence.location: PDF p. 6, Section 3.6, Eq. (12); p. 18, Appendix C.2, Eq. (17) and Table 7
evidence.detail: Stage 2 combines video/action/tactile flow matching with decoded tactile consistency and contact-event supervision. Weights are 1.0/1.0/1.0/0.5/0.1. Gradients pass through the frozen decoder, and tactile losses exclude the current anchor.

evidence.location: PDF p. 18, Table 8 and Appendix C.2
evidence.detail: Both stages use AdamW at 1×10−4, cosine scheduling, 1×10−2 weight decay, 20 epochs, bfloat16, and seed 42. Batch/accumulation settings are 32/1 and 8/2. Initialization uses Wan2.2-TI2V-5B and an aligned ActionDiT checkpoint.

evidence.location: PDF p. 6, Section 3.6; pp. 15–16, Appendix A.6; p. 14, Table 4
evidence.detail: Actions are seven-dimensional joint-position targets with horizon 32. Video geometry uses 33 aligned frames subsampled to nine. Default inference uses 20 denoising steps and feedback after each executed chunk. Decoded tactile futures do not correct actions online.

evidence.location: PDF p. 6, Section 4.1; p. 19, Appendix D.1; p. 20, Appendix E
evidence.detail: The platform is an Agilex Piper with bilateral Xense G1-WS sensors and overhead/wrist cameras, synchronized at 30 Hz. Each task has 300 demonstrations averaging about 500 frames; no explicit demonstration split is stated.

evidence.location: PDF p. 8, Table 2, Chip/Cherry/Wiping/Twirling/Avg. columns and Section 4.2
evidence.detail: TacWAM scores 90.0/70.0/75.0/65.0%, averaging 75.0%. Strongest task baselines are RDP 50.0%, π0.5 60.0%, π0.5 35.0%, and RDP 35.0%. VT-WAM has the strongest baseline average, 37.5%.

evidence.location: PDF p. 8, Evaluation protocol; p. 20, Appendices F–G
evidence.detail: Each method uses one checkpoint and 20 trials per task under matched test-condition sequences and task definitions. Success includes task-specific physical constraints. No confidence intervals or significance tests are reported; numerical pose ranges and cleanliness cutoff are not given.

evidence.location: PDF p. 9, Table 3 and Section 4.3, Without tactile history; pp. 18–19, Appendix C.3
evidence.detail: Full and history-free chip/wiping/mean results are 90.0/75.0/82.5% and 50.0/60.0/55.0%. History removal disables the encoder and contact-event loss while retaining other prediction objectives.

evidence.location: PDF p. 9, Table 3; pp. 9–10, Section 4.3; pp. 16–17, Appendices B.2–B.5
evidence.detail: History-free Attn-AT scores 30.0/45.0/37.5%; Attn-VT scores 10.0/5.0/7.5%. AT exposes tactile futures to actions; VT adds visual–tactile exchange. The authors attribute degradation to target-derived training shortcuts and destabilized co-training.

evidence.location: PDF p. 10, Section 4.3, Future tactile state prediction; p. 11, Figure 4 caption; p. 21, Appendix I
evidence.detail: The text describes closer resultant-force tracking and less lag with history on representative wiping and twirling episodes. No aggregate numerical forecasting error is provided; the curves are diagnostic and do not drive online correction.

evidence.location: PDF pp. 7–8, Baselines; p. 21, Appendix H
evidence.detail: The comparison includes π0.5, Fast-WAM, RDP, and VT-WAM under common task data. Appendix H lists differing optimization configurations, π0.5 horizon 33, and author reimplementations of RDP and VT-WAM.
Stage 2 training uses eight A800-SXM4-80GB GPUs. The documented software includes PyTorch 2.7.1 and CUDA 12.8. No measured generation latency or throughput accompanies the hardware specification.

Raw demonstrations are not released. Training/inference code is promised upon publication under a research-use license, excluding preprocessing, analysis scripts, trained checkpoints, and baseline reimplementation code.
